findings.evidence: Full-time employees who have completed 90 days of continuous service are eligible for the home-office equipment stipend... In addition, eligibility for the workspace stipend depends on several details the reviewer checks one at a time. The workspace must sit inside the employee's primary residence for the stipend to apply... The reviewer confirms the workspace address matches the address already on file with payroll.
findings.fix: Separate the eligibility criteria that applicants need to know from the reviewer procedures into distinct sections or clearly mark which content is for which audience.
findings.violation: The Eligibility section addresses both employees and administrative reviewers within the same section, mixing instructions for applicants with descriptions of what reviewers will do, making it unclear which instructions are for which reader.

findings.evidence: Full-time employees (Eligibility section), the applicant (Restrictions and Exceptions), Staff can request (Program Overview), you submit (Terminology Notes), The requester gets an automatic reminder (Approval Timeline). Also: 'the standard equipment list' (Restrictions and Exceptions) versus 'one device per category' (Restrictions and Exceptions).
findings.fix: Choose one term for each concept and use it consistently throughout, or provide a defined-terms section stating that 'employee', 'applicant', and 'you' refer to the same person.
findings.violation: The document uses five different terms interchangeably for the person applying (employees, applicant, staff, you, requester) and two different terms for the same hardware (equipment, device) without a defined-terms section or stated equivalence, forcing the reader to verify whether terms name the same concept.

findings.evidence: Similarly, the policy applies to one device per category per employee whenever the benefits team confirms that the role genuinely requires a second device because fieldwork regularly takes the employee away from the single fixed desk that the standard equipment list assumes every applicant has for the whole benefit year while the finance office tracks the second device against the same annual amount that the equipment catalog publishes for each category.
findings.fix: State the main rule first in a short sentence, then follow with conditions on separate sentences: 'The policy normally applies to one device per category per employee. However, under these conditions, a second device may apply: [list conditions].'
findings.violation: The sentence opens with the governing rule 'the policy applies to one device per category per employee' but immediately buries it in a cascade of nested conditions and exceptions (whenever... because... while...), forcing the reader to hold the opening rule in mind through a long conditional structure to extract what the actual policy is.

findings.evidence: Current order: (1) Program Overview (2) Eligibility (3) How to Apply (4) Approval Timeline (5) Required Documentation (6) Reimbursement Amounts (7) Restrictions and Exceptions (8) Terminology Notes (9) Request Steps. A reader needing to decide whether to apply would follow: Eligibility → Restrictions and Exceptions → How to Apply → Required Documentation → Timeline. The current order has Restrictions (section 7) appearing after How to Apply (section 3), and Request Steps (section 9) duplicates How to Apply.
findings.fix: Reorder sections to follow the reader's task sequence: Program Overview → Eligibility → Restrictions and Exceptions → How to Apply → Required Documentation → Approval Timeline → Reimbursement Amounts. Remove duplicate information in Request Steps or integrate it into How to Apply.
findings.violation: The document's section order tracks an internal organizational structure rather than the sequence of questions a reader actually works through: readers need to know restrictions before applying, but must read four sections past How to Apply to find them. Also, Request Steps reiterates How to Apply steps far downstream, creating confusion about which section to follow.

findings.evidence: 71-word sentence, 5 subordinate-clause markers: Similarly, the policy applies to one device per category per employee whenever the benefits team confirms that the role genuinely requires a second device because fieldwork regularly takes the employee away from the single fixed desk that the standard equipment list assumes every applicant has for the whole benefit year while the finance office tracks the second device against the same annual amount that the equipment catalog publishes for each category.
findings.fix: Split the sentence at a subordinate-clause boundary.
findings.violation: The sentence runs to 71 words with 5 subordinate-clause markers, longer than the reader can hold in mind on a single pass.

findings.evidence: The determination of stipend eligibility happens before any payment goes out. (Should be: We determine eligibility or Reviewers determine eligibility before any payment goes out.) The escalation of repeat requests happens automatically within the same quarter. (Should be: We escalate repeat requests automatically or The system escalates repeat requests automatically.)
findings.fix: Replace abstract-noun subjects with concrete actors: 'Reviewers determine stipend eligibility before any payment goes out' and 'The benefits team escalates repeat requests automatically within the same quarter.'
findings.violation: Two sentences name abstract processes (determination, escalation) as subjects instead of the actual people or organization performing them, obscuring accountability and leaving the reader unsure who is responsible for these actions.

findings.evidence: You record the stipend item on the request form. Finance reconciles the stipend item against the request log each month. Payroll releases the stipend item amount after that monthly review. Also, you submit the request in the portal. You track its status there until the payment clears.
findings.fix: Either rename the section to describe its actual content (e.g., 'Process and Roles') or separate the content: move employee-facing actions to How to Apply or a separate Employee Checklist section, and move Finance/Payroll information to an administrative procedures section not meant for applicants.
findings.violation: The section titled 'Terminology Notes' actually describes process steps involving three unrelated actors (employee, Finance, Payroll) with no signal connecting them or explaining how their roles relate. A reader finishing the section cannot name a single coherent theme - is it about terminology, employee actions, finance processes, or payroll procedures?

findings.evidence: In addition, eligibility for the workspace stipend depends on several details the reviewer checks one at a time. The workspace must sit inside the employee's primary residence for the stipend to apply. A workspace located in a shared coworking space does not qualify for the stipend under this section. A workspace used only occasionally for calls does not meet the bar the stipend policy sets. The reviewer confirms the workspace address matches the address already on file with payroll. A workspace shared with a roommate can still qualify if the desk area belongs to the employee alone. The stipend covers only the equipment placed inside that confirmed workspace, nothing located elsewhere in the home. A workspace that changes address during the benefit year needs a fresh confirmation before the stipend continues. The reviewer logs every workspace confirmation in the same shared tracking sheet the benefits team maintains. A workspace confirmation from more than one year ago no longer satisfies the stipend requirement on its own.
findings.fix: Split the paragraph into two: one stating all workspace-eligibility rules as conditions applicants must meet, another describing reviewer verification procedures in sequence. Or add clear topic sentences and transition signals: 'To qualify, your workspace must meet these eligibility rules: [list rules]. The reviewer will confirm: [list verification steps].'
findings.violation: Sentences alternate between workspace-eligibility rules and reviewer-procedure descriptions without a coherent topic thread. Subjects jump between 'workspace' (rules for applicants to understand) and 'reviewer' (procedures administrators follow) with no sentence establishing or signaling which topic is which, forcing the reader to re-identify the subject and purpose at each sentence boundary.

findings.evidence: 71-word sentence: Similarly, the policy applies to one device per category per employee whenever the benefits team confirms that the role genuinely requires a second device because fieldwork regularly takes the employee away from the single fixed desk that the standard equipment list assumes every applicant has for the whole benefit year while the finance office tracks the second device against the same annual amount that the equipment catalog publishes for each category.
findings.fix: Move subordinate clauses and modifiers after the main clause, not between its subject and verb.
findings.violation: At 71 words, with 0 comma-set-off clause(s) and 5 subordinate-clause marker(s), the sentence stacks interruptions between its subject and its main verb instead of holding the main clause together.

findings.evidence: Additionally, employees shall retain receipts for one year after the purchase date.
findings.violation: The sentence states a binding requirement using shall or an indirect requirement phrasing instead of must.

findings.fix: Restate the nominalized noun as the sentence's main verb.
findings.violation: The action is buried inside the noun 'evaluation', carried by a generic support verb, instead of stated as the sentence's own main verb.

findings.fix: Split the paragraph so each part covers one topic.
findings.violation: The paragraph exceeds the 150-word scannability threshold.
